pages.title: Money, taxes and the Constitution
pages.sub: Taxes, tariffs, the Federal Reserve and the power of the purse
pages.lede: Article I gives Congress the power to tax, to regulate foreign commerce and to control spending through appropriations, and the Sixteenth Amendment of 1913 allowed taxes on incomes without apportionment. In February 2026 the Supreme Court held that IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs; CBO estimates that about $130 billion was refunded in fiscal 2026, and replacement tariffs were imposed under other statutes. Federal Reserve governors serve fourteen-year terms and may be removed only for cause.
body: Article I gives Congress power 'To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises' and 'To regulate Commerce with foreign Nations', and provides that 'No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law'. [[c-us2-money-text]] It also says: 'No Capitation, or other direct, Tax shall be laid, unless in Proportion to the Census or enumeration herein before directed to be taken.' In Pollock v. Farmers' Loan and Trust Co. (1895) the Court held, 5-4, that taxes on the income of personal property were direct taxes, which therefore had to be apportioned. [[c-us2-money-pollock]] The Sixteenth Amendment, passed by Congress on 2 July 1909 and ratified on 3 February 1913, provides: 'The Congress shall have power to lay and collect taxes on incomes, from whatever source derived, without apportionment among the several States, and without regard to any census or enumeration.' [[c-us2-money-16]] In fiscal 2026 individual income taxes brought in $2,844 billion, more than half of federal receipts of $5,403 billion. [[c-us2-money-receipts]] [[c-us2-money-cbo]] The general taxing and spending power is discussed in US2.2.

The President had imposed 'trafficking' tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China and worldwide 'reciprocal' tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). On 20 February 2026, in Learning Resources v. Trump, the Court held 6-3 that 'IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs'. Chief Justice Roberts wrote for six justices on that holding, but only Gorsuch and Barrett joined the parts relying on the major questions doctrine, which therefore did not command a majority. Justice Kagan, joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, wrote that 'the ordinary tools of statutory interpretation amply support that result'. Justice Kavanaugh, joined by Thomas and Alito, dissented, arguing that statutory text, history and precedent show that IEEPA authorizes tariffs and that the major questions doctrine should not apply to foreign-affairs statutes; Thomas, in a separate dissent, argued that the nondelegation doctrine, which forbids delegating 'core legislative power', does not reach tariffs. [[c-us2-money-learning]]

The administration turned to other statutes. It imposed a 10% surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 from 24 February 2026 (an announced increase to 15%, the statute's maximum, was not put into effect); on 7 May 2026 the Court of International Trade held, 2-1, that the proclamation improperly invoked Section 122's balance-of-payments authority, granting relief only to the three plaintiffs it found to have standing. The Federal Circuit stayed that judgment pending appeal on 11 June 2026, and as of 12 October 2026 the appeal was undecided. The duties expired on 24 July 2026. [[c-us2-money-122]] That day new Section 301 tariffs of 10% or 12.5% took effect on imports from 60 trading partners. Twenty-five states sued in the Court of International Trade on 3 August 2026. On 19 August the court stayed their case while it decided a sample case, In re Section 301 Forced Labor Cases, which a panel heard on 30 September; as of 12 October 2026 no decision had been issued and the duties remained in effect. [[c-us2-money-301]] CBO estimates that about $130 billion in IEEPA tariffs was refunded during fiscal 2026; customs duties fell by $22 billion, or 11 percent, to $172 billion, and the year's deficit was $1,993 billion. [[c-us2-money-cbo]]

The Federal Reserve was 'created in 1913 by the Federal Reserve Act', and its decisions 'do not require approval by the President'. Its governors serve 'fourteen years' unless 'sooner removed for cause by the President'. [[c-us2-money-fed]] That protection was at stake in Trump v. Cook (US2.12), where the Court refused to let the President remove Governor Lisa Cook while her case continued. [[c-us2-admin-cook]] On spending, in Department of State v. AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition (26 September 2025) the Court stayed a lower-court order, saying that the government 'has made a sufficient showing that the Impoundment Control Act precludes respondents' suit', brought under the Administrative Procedure Act, while adding that its order 'should not be read as a final determination on the merits'. Justice Kagan, dissenting with Justices Sotomayor and Jackson, wrote that 'that result conflicts with the separation of powers'. [[c-us2-money-impound]] The budget and appropriations process is covered in US2.3.

pages.title: Politics in practice
pages.lede: The Constitution makes no provision for political parties, and Washington warned against 'the spirit of party'. Since 2010 the courts have held that independent spending, including by corporations, does not corrupt, and have struck down limits on contributions to groups that spend only independently; in 2023-24 independent expenditures reached $4.4 billion, and in June 2026 the Supreme Court struck down limits on parties' coordinated spending. Pew found in 2022 that the parties in Congress were farther apart, on average, than at any time in 50 years.
body: The Constitution makes no provision for political parties, and in his Farewell Address, dated '19th September 1796', Washington warned 'against the baneful effects of the spirit of party'. [[c-us2-pol-parties]] In Citizens United v. FEC (21 January 2010), discussed in US2.9, Justice Kennedy held that 'independent expenditures, including those made by corporations, do not give rise to corruption or the appearance of corruption'. [[c-us2-pol-cu]] Two months later, on 26 March 2010, the D.C. Circuit held in SpeechNow.org v. FEC that 'contributions to groups that make only independent expenditures cannot corrupt or create the appearance of corruption', and that contribution limits were unconstitutional as applied to individuals' contributions to SpeechNow. [[c-us2-pol-speechnow]] The FEC calls 'Political committees that make only independent expenditures' Super PACs; they may accept unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, labor organizations and other political committees, but not from foreign nationals, federal contractors, national banks or federally chartered corporations. [[c-us2-pol-superpacs]]

In 2023-24 independent expenditures reported to the FEC totaled $4.4 billion, of which independent expenditure-only committees accounted for $2.7 billion. [[c-us2-pol-fec-ie]] Those committees received $5,096.9 million, against $2,012.0 million for presidential candidates, $2.3 billion for House candidates and $1.5 billion for Senate candidates. [[c-us2-pol-fec-receipts]] Opinion on the law remains split. Floyd Abrams defends Citizens United: 'The Citizens United ruling is rooted in the First Amendment. That is its basis, its only basis.' Richard Hasen argues that it 'amplified and solidified other significant, incoherent aspects of its campaign finance jurisprudence'. [[c-us2-pol-cf-debate]] On 30 June 2026, in NRSC v. FEC, Justice Kavanaugh, for six justices, held that 'FECA's political-party coordinated-expenditure limits violate the First Amendment' and declared: 'To the extent that Colorado II has retained any vitality, it is now overruled.' Justice Kagan, joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, dissented: 'But today, the Court rewrites the rules, to allow circumvention of the contribution limits.' [[c-us2-pol-nrsc]]

Under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995, as amended in 2007, registrants file quarterly reports; an organization lobbying through its own employees is exempt if its lobbying expenses do not exceed $16,000 a quarter, the threshold in effect from 2025. [[c-us2-pol-lda]] Inside Congress, each House member may employ 'not more than 18 permanent employees' and 'not more than 4 additional employees'. [[c-us2-pol-staff]]

Using DW-NOMINATE scores built from roll-call votes, Pew Research Center reported in 2022 that, 'On average, Democrats and Republicans are farther apart ideologically today than at any time in the past 50 years'. Since 2002 no House Democrat has been more conservative than any House Republican, and since 2004 the same has held in the Senate. The average House Republican moved from 0.25 in 1971-72 to nearly 0.51 in 2021-22, the average House Democrat from about -0.31 to -0.38; as the description of a Pew chart puts it, 'Republicans have moved further to the right than Democrats have to the left.'
